page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.se1.xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine provisioned on the KVM hypervisor. It is powered by a 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon 8269CY processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture. The instance delivers 4 vCPUs mapped across 2 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The CPU configuration features a 35 MB L3 cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and supports vector instructions including AVX and AVX-512F. The hardware profile includes 32.0 GB of memory, representing an allocation of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance is not bundled with local storage or hardware accelerators, and it features a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps with no complimentary public IPv4 addresses included.

Benchmark results place the processing and memory subsystems predominantly in the lower performance tiers. The system achieved a Geekbench multi-core score of 1990.0 and a single-core score of 918.0, categorized in the bottom 10% of tested systems. Multi-core compute benchmarks recorded 2931.93 in stress-ng and an overall PassMark CPU score of 3629.17. Large-block memory transfers reached 20.19 GB/sec for uncached read operations and 18.14 GB/sec for write operations. Data processing tasks demonstrated similar throughput limitations, with single-threaded gzip compression achieving 18.88 GB/sec and single-threaded bzip3 decompression registering 7.39 GB/sec.

In operational benchmarks, the instance recorded 2.87 million operations per second in Redis SET operations and a static web serving throughput of 2.41 GB/sec. Lightweight inference with a 135M parameter language model achieved 243.77 tokens/sec during prompt processing and 59.58 tokens/sec for text generation. From a resource perspective, the high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8:1 provides cost efficiency for services requiring substantial in-memory footprints without the expense of higher vCPU counts. However, users must account for the trade-off of modest raw computing performance and the absence of integrated local storage.

Alibaba Cloud ecs.se1.xlarge is primarily suited for memory-centric operational workloads that do not demand extensive computational speed. Appropriate deployments include distributed in-memory caching tiers such as Redis, lightweight relational databases, and background ETL processes that process moderate batches within memory.
